<reason>Side B (PRO) won a closely fought, high-quality exchange. The decisive issue: A's endgame burden attack repeatedly claimed the proposition says AI "will" eliminate more jobs, and accused B of retreating from "will" to "likely" — but the motion as written only requires "likely." B corrected this in B4.1 ("the motion is that net loss is likely"), which undercut A's strongest closing line and exposed A's demand for a completed payroll census as over-raising the evidentiary bar. On substance, both sides had real material: A's ATM/spreadsheet elasticity pattern and "churn, not net loss" framing were sharp, but B's distinguishing mechanism — previous tools automated tasks while human cognition stayed the scarce input, whereas this tool fills extra demand via inference itself ("the same model drafts them"; "a verifier on three workflows is not the junior class restored") — was never squarely neutralized; A's verification-scales-with-output counter remained an assertion of similar weight. On the policy half, A's own concession that portable benefits and insurance are worthwhile anyway made B's lag-and-asymmetry argument ("institutions take years; designing programs in a professional-class slump") hard to beat, and B's dismissal of A's monitoring indicators ("vacancies move after the freeze") went largely unanswered. Both sides used proper Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structure and answered pressure directly. A's rhetoric was crisper ("the pattern beats the worry"), but B made the debate easier to decide on the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.1–B4.5: B directly answered A's burden pressure by pointing out the motion requires likelihood, not proven-zero elasticity, then turned the copywriter question back on A — liability sign-off is not those workers' job, and extra output drafted by the same model does not rehire them — leaving A's verification response looking thin.</best_rebuttal>
